title: A Postcards for the Glasshouse
premise: Silas Blackwood, a woman who writes weekly postcards to a house that burned down eleven years ago, learns that her childhood home in the glasshouse town of Verrow is being auctioned by relatives she hasn't spoken to since the fire. Returning under the pretext of cataloguing the estate, she discovers her late grandmother's letters — proof that the fire that killed Silas's father was no accident, and that the family quietly agreed to bury the truth. As the auction date approaches, Silas must choose between exposing the family's arrangement, which would destroy her fragile reconciliation with her sister Maren, and letting the house — and the justice owed to her father — be sold off forever. In the end she reads the truth aloud at the auction itself, loses the house, and gains something rarer: her sister's hand in hers, and a postcard finally addressed to a place that exists.
about_author: Hazel Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing the correspondence of estranged families in rural county probate offices. She writes about the letters people send to places that no longer exist, and the debts that outlive the houses they were incurred in.

chapters.title: The Address That Isn't There
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. We meet her in her rented room, writing her 573rd postcard to a burned-down address, mailing it to a post office that returns nothing. Establish her tenant-like existence: temporary job, unpacked boxes, a life arranged for departure. Emotional beat: grief disguised as habit, the comfort of rituals that ask nothing of her.

chapters.title: A Notice in the Gazette
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A legal notice names Blackwood House — her childhood home — as entering auction. Her aunt Odette's name appears as executor. Silas rereads the notice until the ink blurs, then packs a bag in twenty minutes. Emotional beat: the past converting from memory into obligation; fear sharpened into resolve.

chapters.title: The Road to Verrow
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, with a bus conversation from a stranger who knew her father. Verrow has changed and hasn't; the glasshouse ruins still glint on the hill. She arrives at Blackwood House and finds her sister Maren already there, cataloguing for the estate sale. Emotional beat: the shock of home as a stranger's property, and of Maren as a stranger wearing a sister's face.

chapters.title: Inventory of a Family
chapters.summary: Alternating Silas and Maren POV. The sisters catalogue rooms together, trading barbed courtesies. Each object carries a different memory for each of them — the same piano, two entirely different childhoods. Emotional beat: the realization that they survived the same fire into different truths.

chapters.title: What Odette Keeps Locked
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Aunt Odette arrives to supervise, charming and controlling, steering the sisters away from the study. Silas notices the study door is newly locked, its key on Odette's chain. Emotional beat: suspicion blooming in the soil of old deference — Silas realizes she has been managed her whole life.

chapters.title: Maren's Version of the Fire
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Flashbacks: Maren was fourteen, Silas nine, the night the glasshouse annex burned and their father died. Maren remembers their father's last argument — with Odette, not with a stranger. She has spent her life agreeing with the family's official story to keep Odette's financial support. Emotional beat: complicity as a kind of love, and its slow rot.

chapters.title: Postcards, Returned
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. A bundle of Silas's old postcards arrives, forwarded by the post office — every one returned 'addressee unknown' over eleven years. Reading her own words back, she sees how long she's been writing to a ghost instead of the living. Emotional beat: the ritual cracking; grief becoming a question with an answer she's avoided.

chapters.title: The Key Under the Lilac
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Maren, who knows the house's hiding places, watches Silas circle the study. That night she copies Odette's key from a hook in the kitchen and hesitates at the study door — then puts the key under the lilac bush where they hid things as children, letting Silas find it without ever handing it over. Emotional beat: betrayal of Odette as the first honest act of Maren's adulthood.

chapters.title: Letters in Grandmother's Hand
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Inside the study: their grandmother's letters, written before her death, describing the insurance fraud Odette orchestrated — the annex was burned deliberately, and their father, who threatened to expose it, was inside when it went up. Silas reads until dawn. Emotional beat: horror braided with relief — she was right to distrust the story, and right to distrust herself for staying silent.

chapters.title: The Arrangement
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. We see the family machinery from inside: Odette's payments to Maren, her management of the estate, her conviction that she protected the family from ruin — and from Silas's father's 'recklessness.' She is not a monster in her own account; she is a woman who chose order over truth. Emotional beat: chilling self-justification; justice and cruelty wearing the same coat.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Greenhouse
chapters.summary: Silas and Odette, Silas POV. Silas shows Odette the letters in the ruined glasshouse where their father died. Odette neither denies nor confesses; she offers Silas a share of the auction proceeds and the family's continued silence. Emotional beat: the temptation of a clean transactional evil — money in exchange for burying her father a second time.

chapters.title: What Maren Owes
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Odette confronts Maren about the missing key, threatening to end the allowance that pays for Maren's daughter's school. Maren realizes her whole adult life has been purchased with her silence. She doesn't yet choose — but she stops sleeping. Emotional beat: duty revealed as a debt with compounding interest.

chapters.title: An Appraisal of Small Things
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The auctioneer's appraiser arrives; Silas watches her childhood priced line by line. She begins secretly photographing documents and hiding copies. A tender, unexpected connection forms with the appraiser, Tomas, who notices what she's doing and says nothing. Emotional beat: an ally found by accident; love arriving when she'd stopped looking.

chapters.title: The Sister's Bargain
chapters.summary: Silas and Maren, alternating POV. The sisters finally speak plainly at the lake where their father taught them to skip stones. Maren admits what she knew and what she was paid to forget. Silas asks her to stand with her at the auction and say the truth aloud. Maren asks for time. Emotional beat: the raw, unglamorous work of forgiveness begun, not finished.

chapters.title: Odette's Countermove
chapters.summary: Odette's POV. Odette discovers the copied documents, accelerates the auction date, and begins quietly framing Silas as unstable — the grieving daughter who writes to burned houses. She tells the town Silas has come to disrupt a lawful sale. Emotional beat: watching power operate not through lies but through plausible, well-funded versions of the truth.

chapters.title: The Town That Knew
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Silas visits old neighbors — the fire warden, her father's foreman — and learns they always suspected; the town arranged itself around the same silence as the family. Some beg her to let it lie. One, the foreman, gives her the missing letter her father mailed the day he died. Emotional beat: complicity at civic scale; the loneliness of being the only one who wants the truth out loud.

chapters.title: Her Father's Last Postcard
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. The father's final letter, never delivered, names Odette and the fraud explicitly and asks the grandmother to protect his daughters. Silas understands now why she writes postcards: she inherited the habit from a man whose last act was to write the truth down. Emotional beat: inheritance redefined — not the house, not the money, but the pen.

chapters.title: The Night Before the Auction
chapters.summary: Maren's POV. Odette offers Maren a final choice: a signed statement discrediting Silas, or the end of every payment. Maren spends the night walking the house, touching every room, then burns the statement Odette prepared and writes her own — the truth, in her hand. Emotional beat: love against duty, decided at 3 a.m. in a kitchen that smells of lilacs.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Silas POV, climax. Bidders fill the lawn. When the auctioneer calls the house, Silas takes the podium instead, and reads her father's letter and the grandmother's letters aloud. Maren steps up beside her and confirms it. The room fractures; Odette walks out; the auction collapses into chaos. Emotional beat: terror transfigured — the truth spoken is smaller and larger than she imagined.

chapters.title: What the Law Does and Doesn't
chapters.summary: Silas and Maren POV. The letters go to a journalist and the insurance commission; the legal machinery moves slowly and imperfectly — Odette may never face a courtroom, but the family's arrangement is dead, the sale voided by the executor's exposure. Emotional beat: justice outside the law is not a verdict but a refusal to keep the secret; imperfect, and still real.

chapters.title: The House Sells Anyway
chapters.summary: Silas's POV. Months later, Blackwood House sells at a quiet private sale — to a young family, not to Odette. Silas walks it one last time, leaves her father's letter framed on the study desk, and takes only the piano bench. Emotional beat: letting the house go without letting the truth go; ownership redefined as witness.

chapters.title: A Postcard for the Living
chapters.summary: Silas's POV, resolution. In her new apartment — owned, not rented — Silas writes her 574th postcard and addresses it to Maren, who lives two streets away. She mails it anyway, because some letters are for the sending, not the distance. Maren's reply arrives the next day: one line, 'Come for supper.' Emotional beat: grief completed into love; the tenant finally home.
